blocks.title: Waterfall model
blocks.text: The Waterfall model is a straightforward approach in which each phase of the project must be completed before the next begins, like a waterfall flowing from one level to the next. It is linear and sequential: you move through the phases in order without going back once a phase is complete (Fig. 1.2).

items: Requirements: gather and document what the software must do.
Design: plan how the software will be built and look.
Testing: check for and fix problems or bugs.
Deployment: release the software to users.
Maintenance: update it and fix issues after it is in use.

blocks.caption: Waterfall: benefits and limitations
rows: Simple and easy to understand: clear, distinct phases
Inflexible: going back to change a finished phase is difficult and costly
Sequential process: one phase at a time, easy to manage and track
Not ideal for complex projects with evolving requirements
Suitable for small projects with clear, fixed requirements
Risk and uncertainty: assumes all requirements are known at the start

blocks.alt: Under the title Waterfall (Plan Driven), seven dark blue arrows step down from left to right: Requirements, Analysis, Design, Implementation, Testing, Delivery and Maintenance. Short task lists sit under the arrows, and a long arrow labelled Project Timeline runs along the bottom.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.2: Waterfall Model (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.2).
blocks.long_description: Tasks printed under the phases: Requirements: define project scope, stakeholder interviews, user research, requirements gathering, kick-off meeting. Design: high-level design, design review, design revisions, stakeholder approval. Implementation: dev phase 1, review, dev phase 2, review. Testing: testing, revisions. Delivery: deployment.

blocks.text: The term Waterfall was first introduced by Dr. Winston W. Royce in 1970, but he did not advocate its use without iteration.
